title: Fault-tolerant resource estimation for ground-state preparation via Lindblad simulation
authors: Marius Bothe, Patrick Schoepf, Nick S. Blunt
abstract: Recent advances in algorithms for simulating Lindblad dynamics have clarified their theoretical potential for state preparation, but their practicality in the early fault-tolerant regime and beyond remains uncertain. In this work, we address this by investigating the cost of preparing ground states of the fermionic Hubbard model, following the single-ancilla approach of [Phys. Rev. Research 6, 033147 (2024)]. We derive rigorous error bounds including constant prefactors, and compare to empirical error behavior and practical convergence parameters obtained from circuit-level simulations. We find that empirically chosen parameters can reduce the required resources by orders of magnitude, resulting in an estimated $7.7 \times 10^8$ T gates to perform one unit of time evolution targeting the low-energy subspace of a 36-site fermionic Hubbard model. We identify the accurate filtering of energy transitions as the main source of this cost.
summary: This paper analyzes the resource cost of preparing the ground state of the fermionic Hubbard model using Lindblad simulation techniques. It derives rigorous error bounds by analyzing the approximations involved in simulating the energy-filtering process. The results provide a concrete, albeit large, gate count estimate, highlighting energy transition filtering as the main computational hurdle.
main_problem: The paper investigates the practical resource cost and feasibility of using Lindblad simulation techniques for preparing the ground state of quantum many-body systems in the early fault-tolerant quantum computing regime.

method: The authors employ a dilation-based simulation approach, deriving rigorous error bounds for the approximation of the Lindblad evolution via quadrature and Trotterization techniques.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The energy-domain filter function ˆf as well as its Dirichlet kernel approximations for different numbers of sample points MS. The colored areas begin at the smallest possible energy transitions to and from the ground state, ∆. The blue area indicates transitions that dissipate energy (cooling) and the red area indicates transitions that increase the energy (heating).

Figure 2. Comparison of jump operators, A, in the eigenbasis of the 2-site Hubbard Hamiltonian with U = 4 and open boundary conditions. The left operator acts only on the spin-down section, whereas the right operator acts on a linear combination of both. The axis labels indicate the eigenstates in order from lowest to highest energy, such that the top-right triangular matrix contains the desired energy transitions. Note that the two-spin mixer on the right is no longer ergodic in the Sz = 0, 2-particle sector since it is missing the top-left transition.

Figure 3. Energy error relative to the ground-state energy as a function of time, for the 2-site Hubbard model with U = 4, with different levels of amplitude damping noise applied. The system is initialized in a Sz = 0, two-particle state, but drifts into other particle sectors due to the noise, resulting in a different fixed point.

Figure 4. Example energy trajectory in a state vector simulation for a 6-site one-dimensional Hubbard model with U = 4 and open boundary conditions. Vertical dashed lines indicate jumps, i.e. when the ancilla state was measured in the |1⟩-state.

Figure 5. Energy convergence in the density matrix simulation of the 2-site Hubbard model with U = 4 for different values of the steepness parameter a. Smaller values of a speed up the evolution as they enable more dissipation, but they also increase leakage into higher-energy states.
